question_text: Why use multiple different values of decoupling capacitors (e.g., two 4.7µF, one 1µF, and one 0.1µF) in parallel instead of just a single 10µF capacitor?
answer_text: It reduces overall Equivalent Series Resistance (ESR) and widens the bandwidth of noise filtering across different frequencies.
explanation_text: Large capacitors (4.7µF) act as bulk storage for low-frequency current spikes but have a low Self-Resonant Frequency (SRF), meaning they become inductive (useless) at high frequencies. Small capacitors (0.1µF) hold less charge but have a very high SRF, filtering out high-frequency noise. By placing them in parallel, their individual V-shaped impedance curves overlap, creating a wide, flat band of low impedance across a huge frequency range. Additionally, putting components in parallel divides their ESR and ESL, lowering total impedance.
bonus_question_text: What is a risk of placing multiple different capacitor values in parallel?
bonus_answer_text: Anti-resonance. The inductive parasitics of the large capacitor can resonate with the capacitive parasitics of the small capacitor at a specific frequency, creating an unwanted high-impedance spike.
